outputs.L1:
I thank the spiders' webs and the circus dancers who stain our eyes with rapid movements, and who grant our handcuffs the license to make no distinction between night and day, or love and hate.

No one will ever know the sum of our arduous daily separations, from bed to work. These pillars, in truth, belong to you, for I have never counted them, nor do I know any better than you where they stand, or in what country they still endure. We may gather all our cares into a loaf of bread and tender French kisses, go to the movies, and watch the splashing milk upon the screen imitate the forest bathed in moonlight. Why all this fuss about the patrons turning to feathers, discharging their notions of nobility on the evening news? There are no lights within the theater—only soft snow drifting from the balcony, which is the little red schoolhouse where all of this began.

In truth, it was because of you that I did not attend as often as I should have. I was too embarrassed to face you across the clay-modeling tables, for I always felt that the clay in your hands was a cartoon rendering of my teenage years—dear slippery-fish ladies of the sleepy west.

Do not forget: my early life shall be yours as well, with all its self-descriptions of poetic justice. The tiny creatures we write about can describe themselves in the moss we leave behind.
outputs.L2:
I offer gratitude to the webs spun by spiders and to the performers who twirl in circus rings, blurring our vision with their swift motions and giving our shackles permission to draw no line between darkness and light, or between affection and loathing.

The total of our difficult daily partings—from mattress to labor—will remain unknown to everyone. These columns are yours by right, for I've never tallied them, nor do I understand any better than you where they stand or which nation still holds them. Every worry we carry can be tucked inside a slice of bread and deep kisses; we can head to the cinema and observe how the milk spilling across the screen mimics woodland bathed in lunar glow. Why get worked up over the customers transforming into plumes, unloading their notions of grandeur onto the nightly broadcast? The playhouse holds no illumination—only gentle snowfall drifting from the upper seats, which is the small crimson schoolhouse where every bit of this originated.

Truthfully, you were the reason I showed up less frequently than I ought to have. Sitting opposite you at the pottery-shaping benches filled me with too much shame, because the clay you molded always struck me as a comic-strip rendering of my adolescence, oh you elusive, fish-like women of the drowsy western lands.

Remember this: my youth shall belong to you as well, complete with its own accounts of poetic fairness. Those miniature beings that fill our writing are able to portray themselves within the moss we abandon in our wake.
outputs.L3:
**A Gratitude Woven from Threads and Motion**

I find myself grateful, first of all, for the webs that spiders spin—those delicate architectures that catch the light—and equally grateful for the circus dancers whose bodies move so quickly that they seem to dissolve the ordinary borders of the world. In their spinning, night bleeds into day, and love becomes indistinguishable from hate. It is as though their motion reminds me that the divisions we cling to are more porous than we imagine.

Between the bed I leave each morning and the work I return to, there are countless small departures, none of which anyone bothers to count. They accumulate silently, these daily separations. And the pillars that hold up whatever it is we've built together—those we own in common, yet neither of us could say where they stand. They support us from some location we've never located, a shared possession lost to both our maps.

Still, I have learned that the weight of everyday concerns can be lifted and remade into something simpler, something nourishing: a loaf of bread, a kiss, the flickering light of a movie. On the screen, the images gather themselves into the shape of a forest touched by moonlight, and for a moment the mundane becomes luminous.

I should confess that I have been staying away, and the reason is embarrassment. When I imagine showing up, I feel myself shrinking into something flattened and unreal—a cartoon rendering of my own adolescence, that awkward self who was shaped and unsettled by the slippery-fish ladies, those elusive figures who slipped through my early years and left me formless.

And yet I want you to have all of it. My beginnings will belong to you as much as to me. I will hand over the words I once used to describe myself, and I will leave behind my traces—small marks pressed into the world—so faint that only the tiniest creatures could read them, spelling out my story in the soft green language of the moss.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem full of dreamlike, disconnected imagery about love, memory, and separation, addressed to a mysterious "you."
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Water Kept

You left through a door that was actually a season. I remember this because the hinges smelled like October and my hands forgot how to close.

There is a room in me where you are still folding laundry made of light. The socks never match. This is how I know it was real.

---

Once, you spoke my name and three birds fell asleep inside the word. I have been carrying them ever since, careful, careful, the way one carries a bowl of borrowed rain across a country that keeps rearranging its rivers.

Do you remember the piano we found underwater? How we played it anyway, and the notes came up as bubbles, each one holding a smaller version of us, waving?

---

Memory is a house where all the mirrors face the garden. I walk its halls at the hour when clocks lose their nerve. Here is your coat, still warm with an argument we never finished. Here is the staircase that descends only into afternoons we did not have.

You are the punctuation missing from every sentence I try to end.

---

When you go, the moon becomes a coin someone flipped and forgot to catch. Everything is suspended. The cat is halfway through the wall. The tea is halfway to my mouth. Half of me is still turning to tell you something I have already forgotten, something urgent, something about the color of your absence—

which is the blue of a photograph left too long in the sun,

which is the sound of a name being slowly returned to the alphabet,

which is, I think, simply *you*,

walking backward through the orchard,

taking each blossom with you,

until the branches are only branches,

until the tree remembers it was always

just my two open hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of automatic writing in the style of the Surrealists, blending nonsensical images like spider webs, circus dancers, handcuffs, and clay modeling tables.
counterfactuals.output:
The clay remembers what the fingers forgot, and the fingers remember nothing, they are busy elsewhere, threading themselves through spider silk that hangs from the chandelier of a mouth that never closes. I walked into the room where the tables were breathing. Each modeling table exhaled a small gray lung of dust and on the dust a circus dancer had left her footprint, one footprint only, the other foot she had traded for a handcuff, a beautiful silver handcuff she wore like a bracelet, like a promise, like the last word of a sentence nobody would finish.

Spider, spider, weaving the ceiling into a hammock for the tired moon—the moon comes down at midnight to sleep in the webs and the dancers spin around it, tuk-tuk on their pointe shoes, tuk-tuk, and the handcuffs jingle like church keys, like the keys to a church made entirely of thumbs.

I pressed my palm into the clay and the clay pressed back. This is the agreement we made without words: I would give it a shape and it would give me a wound. Fair trade. The web slid down and wrapped my wrist. Now I too wore the silver, now I too was married to the trapeze, and the ringmaster with the face of an overturned bucket announced me to a crowd of empty chairs that clapped by falling over.

Where did the dancers go? Into the clay. They are always going into the clay. Watch: a leg emerges from the modeling table like a swimmer surfacing, a leg wearing one handcuff, and the spider descends to measure it for a stocking made of thread and screaming.

Somewhere a bell. Somewhere the circus folds itself into a matchbox and the matchbox into a tooth and the tooth into the soft wet dark behind my thinking. The web says *stay*. The clay says *become*. The handcuff says nothing, it only shines, it only holds two things together that never wanted to touch—my hand and the hour, the dancer and the floor, the dream and its own long tail disappearing under the door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem that reads like a letter to an old lover, mixing childhood memories of school with absurd, illogical metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# Letter to the One Who Sat Behind Me

Dear you,

I still keep the chalk dust of your laughter
in a jar I labeled *do not open until the ceiling forgets us.*

Remember multiplication tables?
You were the number that refused to be divided,
and I was the long division no one could finish,
carrying the one across whole summers.

Your hair smelled like the color blue
before we knew blue was a lie
the sky tells to feel important.

We passed notes shaped like small countries.
Mine always seceded before reaching your desk.
The teacher said *pay attention*
but attention was a coat I'd already loaned
to the boy who drowned in the aquarium of your eyes,
which, for the record, contained no water,
only the low hum of a vending machine
dispensing hearts that were slightly expired.

I loved you the way a fire drill loves a Tuesday—
sudden, loud, and secretly hoping
the building would stay standing.

Do you still owe the library
that book about the ocean?
I think it grew legs.
I think it walks the halls now
looking for the version of us
that did the homework, that spelled *forever* right
on the very first try
instead of erasing until the paper wore thin
as the excuse I gave for never calling.

They repainted our classroom.
The walls no longer hold the shape
of a boy leaning toward a girl
like a comma leaning toward the sentence
it was too afraid to end.

If you find the jar,
don't open it.
Let the chalk stay a cloud.
Let the cloud stay somebody's answer
to a question the teacher never asked,

which was, of course,
*where does the recess bell go
when it finishes ringing?*

I think I know now.
It goes wherever you went.
It rings there still.

Yours in permanent marker,
the desk in the third row
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness poem that defies logic, moving between night and day, love and hate, movies, bread, and snow in a theater.
counterfactuals.output:
**Reel of Salt and Sugar**

Night unbuttons its coat and the sun falls out,
a warm coin rolling under the theater seats—
I am buttering the dark,
I am hating you tenderly, the way you fold
a movie into your pocket and call it morning.

Someone is baking noon in the projector.
The bread rises through the ceiling of every dream,
crust of dawn, crumb of midnight,
and love says, *don't*—
and love says, *again*—
two contradictions holding the same doorknob.

Snow begins in aisle seven.
It does not know it is indoors.
It falls on the popcorn, it falls on the ushers,
it falls on the black-and-white lovers
who kiss in a language of flickering,
who hate in a language of flickering,
who are the same frame stuttered a thousand times.

I loved you at 3 a.m. in a bakery of noon.
I hated you across the aisle
where the snow made a small quiet field
and the movie ran backward
so the dead deer stood up
and the toast leapt back into wheat
and the night sky remembered it was a screen
and the screen remembered it was crumbs
and the crumbs remembered they were you,
scattered across the floor of some feeling
I could not fold, could not butter, could not
switch off—

so I sat there
eating the light,
eating the cold,
watching two seasons argue over one seat,
while day and night traded coats in the projector's throat
and love, the buttered saboteur,
melted quietly into the reel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde prose poem addressed to "slippery-fish ladies of the sleepy west" that reflects on teenage years, art class, and poetic justice.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for the Slippery-Fish Ladies of the Sleepy West

Slippery-fish ladies of the sleepy west, I am writing to you from the drowned end of adolescence, where the clocks all melt like the clocks we were told not to copy in art class, though we copied them anyway, badly, our Dalís sweating in tempera.

You knew us then—scaled and darting, impossible to hold. Every teacher a net. Every net a lesson in poetic justice: the way the boy who mocked my still-life apples grew up to sell insurance beneath fluorescent light, while my rotten fruit hangs, framed, in the museum of what I refused to become.

*

Listen: I have carried the smell of turpentine like a first religion. The smock that never fit. The kiln we feared would eat us. Ladies, do you remember how we were all *becoming*—unfinished, gessoed, primed for a picture nobody could yet see?

The west was always sleepy. The sun a lazy egg yolk breaking over strip malls. And we, the fish, believed we'd swim clean out of that watercolor town, out past the horizon line our instructor drew too low, insisting *this is where the world ends.*

*

But here is the justice, and it is poetic:

The bullies became the bullied by their mortgages. The pretty ones learned mirrors are just water that forgot how to move. And the strange girl—the one who painted her self-portrait with a fish's face—she is the one still here, still slick, still swimming, still refusing to be caught by anything so dull as an ending.

*

Slippery-fish ladies, wherever you gleam—
in the sleepy west, in the wet dark, in the space
between the brushstroke and the wall—

keep swimming.

The still-life was never still.
The fruit was always about to fall.
And we were always, always
too quick
to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
